Topology

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Geometry and topology
OurBigBook.com Words: 23k Articles: 403
Topology studies topological spaces through open sets and continuous maps. Its central equivalence is a homeomorphism: a bijection that preserves continuity in both directions. This lets us distinguish spaces by connectedness or compactness even when numerical metric values are irrelevant. The open interval (0,1) and the real line have the same topology in this sense, although only the former is a bounded set with its usual metric.
The upper panels show an explicit homeomorphism and the inverse image test for a continuous map. The lower panels exhibit an obstruction to a homeomorphism: removing any point from a circle leaves a connected space, whereas removing an interior point from a closed interval gives two connected components.
Homotopy is a different notion: it varies a continuous map continuously with a parameter and may collapse points. For example, H(x,t)=(1−t)x contracts [0,1] to zero. Thus this closed interval and a singleton have the same homotopy type, but there is no homeomorphism between them because there is no bijection. Homotopy equivalence need not preserve compactness. [ref]
The abstract viewpoint already appears explicitly in Tietze's 1923 paper: he describes topology as the study of properties invariant under invertible continuous maps with continuous inverses, and discusses axioms for neighbourhoods, citing Hausdorff's 1914 book, page 213. [ref]

Topological invariant

Words: 43
Topology OurBigBook.com
A topological invariant is a property or mathematical object preserved by homeomorphisms of topological spaces. Connectedness and compactness are examples. The fundamental group is an invariant up to group isomorphism; it is also preserved up to isomorphism by homotopy equivalence, a stronger invariance property which does not hold for every topological invariant.

End (topology)

Words: 47
Topology OurBigBook.com
An end of a noncompact topological space describes a coherent way to escape every compact subset. For a cofinal compact exhaustion, when one exists, K1​⊆K2​⊆⋯, it is represented by nested connected components of the complements. A connected noncompact manifold is disconnected at infinity when it has more than one end.

Orientability

Words: 342
Topology OurBigBook.com
Orientability asks whether local choices of handedness can agree everywhere on a manifold. On a smooth manifold, an orientation of a smooth manifold chooses an orientation of a vector space for each tangent space, continuously with position. An ordered basis describes the same handedness as another one when the change-of-basis determinant is positive. An oriented atlas implements this condition through positive Jacobian determinants of the smooth transition maps.
A paper strip makes the obstruction visible. Join its short ends without twisting: the resulting untwisted band admits a consistent choice of unit normal. Add a half-turn before joining: on the Möbius band, following the core circle of a Möbius band reverses that choice when you first return to the same point. A local decision about handedness has encountered a global contradiction. The normal reversal around the Möbius core makes this precise for an explicit model.
Both rectangles have coordinates (u,v)∈[0,1]×[−1,1]. The untwisted band identifies (0,v) with (1,v); the Möbius band identifies (0,v) with (1,−v). Across a seam the corresponding local coordinate changes preserve or reverse v, giving determinants +1 and −1. This sign explains the handedness change; the drawing also tracks the two boundary circles of the untwisted band and the single boundary circle of the Möbius band.
For a smooth topological surface embedded in R3, choosing an orientation of a surface is equivalent to choosing a continuous unit normal. This picture is specific to surfaces in three-dimensional space: the general definition uses compatible local orientations, without requiring an embedding. Orientability is a topological invariant, so a homeomorphism cannot turn a Möbius band into a untwisted band. The sphere and torus are orientable surfaces; the Klein bottle is not. [ref]
The distinction matters when a sign has geometric meaning. A signed flux surface integral needs an orientation of a surface, and Stokes theorem relates that choice to the outward-normal-first boundary orientation. Ordinary unsigned surface area does not require orientability. Thus a Möbius band still has a perfectly meaningful area even though it has no continuous global unit normal.
A connected orientable manifold of positive dimension has two possible orientations: reversing every local choice gives the other one. If a manifold has several connected components, each component can be oriented independently when it is orientable. For topological surfaces, a useful obstruction criterion is the presence of a Möbius band: a surface is nonorientable exactly when it contains such a band. [ref]

Non-Hausdorff manifold

Words: 37
Topology OurBigBook.com
A non-Hausdorff manifold is a locally Euclidean topological space for which distinct points need not have disjoint neighborhoods. The real line with two origins is a basic example. Nonseparated algebraic schemes exhibit analogous gluing phenomena, but are not generally topological manifolds.

Stone space

Words: 25
Topology OurBigBook.com
A Stone space is a compact Hausdorff space that is totally disconnected, equivalently a compact Hausdorff space with a basis of clopen sets. The topology on a type space gives an important example.

Tail topology on the natural numbers (τ={∅}∪{{n,n+1,…}:n∈N})

Words: 119 Articles: 1
Topology OurBigBook.com
The nonempty open sets are the upper tails of the natural numbers. Arbitrary nonempty unions select the smallest starting index, and finite intersections select the largest, so these sets form a topology. A map into this space is continuous exactly when the inverse image of every upper tail is open.

Continuous maps between cofinite and tail topologies

Words: 71
Tail topology on the natural numbers OurBigBook.com
For a map f:N→N from the cofinite topology to the tail topology on the natural numbers, continuity is equivalent to every set {n:f(n)≥k} being empty or cofinite. If the image is unbounded, every such set is nonempty and cofinite, so f(n)→∞. If it is bounded, its maximum M exists, and the inverse image of the tail at M forces f(n)=M eventually, with f(n)≤M always. Conversely either condition makes every tail preimage empty or cofinite.

Fell topology

Words: 65
Topology OurBigBook.com
The Fell topology on the closed subsets of a locally compact space has subbasic open sets requiring intersection with an open set or avoidance of a compact set. On a locally compact separable metric space, its sequential convergence says that every convergent subsequence of points from the varying sets has its limit in the limiting set, and every point of the limiting set is approximated by points from the varying sets.

Upper-ray topology on the real line ({∅,R}∪{(a,∞):a∈R})

Words: 66
Topology OurBigBook.com
These sets form a topology: a nonempty union of upper rays is another upper ray, or all of R when their endpoints have no lower bound; a finite intersection of rays has endpoint the maximum of their endpoints. The whole line must be included. The continuous map n↦n from N with the cofinite topology to this space is nonconstant, because each upper ray has cofinite inverse image.

Hyperconnected space

Words: 40
Topology OurBigBook.com
A topological space is hyperconnected if any two nonempty open sets intersect. Every continuous map from a nonempty hyperconnected space to a Hausdorff space is constant: two distinct image points would have disjoint open neighbourhoods whose nonempty inverse images contradict hyperconnectedness. Every infinite set with the cofinite topology is hyperconnected.

Closed cover (X=⋃i​Fi​,Fi​ closed)

Words: 57
Topology OurBigBook.com
A closed cover of a topological space is a family of closed sets whose union is the whole space. A finite closed cover can be used in separation and antipodal arguments: in a metric space, vanishing distance to a closed member means actual membership. Unlike an open cover, a closed cover does not automatically have a partition of unity subordinate to its members.

Partition topology

Words: 80
Topology OurBigBook.com
Given a partition of a set, declare a subset open precisely when it is a union of partition blocks. Arbitrary unions and finite intersections of such unions are again unions of blocks, giving a topology. The quotient map to the block set with its discrete topology pulls that topology back to the original set. For the partition of Z into its two parity classes, the only open sets are the empty set, those two classes, and all of Z.

Finite subsets do not define a topology on an infinite set

Words: 61
Topology OurBigBook.com
On an infinite set, the family consisting of all finite subsets and the whole set need not be closed under arbitrary unions. On Z, the union of the singleton subsets of 2Z is infinite and proper, so this family is not a topology. It must not be confused with the cofinite topology, whose proper open sets have finite complements.

Lower limit topology

Words: 113 Articles: 1
Topology OurBigBook.com
The lower limit topology on R has basis of a topology {[a,b):a<b}. Every such nonempty interval contains a rational, so this topological space is separable. Its topology is finer than the usual Euclidean topology; the one-sided basic neighbourhoods allow its square to have an uncountable discrete antidiagonal.

Sorgenfrey plane

Words: 70
Lower limit topology OurBigBook.com
The Sorgenfrey plane is the product topology on two copies of the Sorgenfrey line. It is separable because Q2 meets every nonempty basic rectangle [a,b)×[c,d). Its antidiagonal {(x,−x):x∈R} is an uncountable discrete subspace: [x,x+ϵ)×[−x,−x+ϵ) meets it only at (x,−x). In a discrete space every dense subset is the whole space, so this subspace is not separable. Thus separability need not pass to subspaces of nonmetrizable spaces.

Symmetric product (Symg(X))

Words: 68
Topology OurBigBook.com
The gth symmetric product of a space X is Symg(X)=Xg/Sg​, where the symmetric group permutes the factors. Its points are unordered g-tuples, with repetitions allowed. Topology OurBigBook.com
The cofinite topology on a set X declares the empty set and all cofinite subsets to be open sets: a nonempty open set may exclude only a finite set of points. There is no assumed metric. On an infinite set, this gives a particularly small collection of open sets while still making every singleton a closed set. On a finite set, every subset has finite complement, so the cofinite topology is the discrete topology.[ref]
For an original example, use X=N>0​ and choose
U=X∖{2,5,8},V=X∖{1,3,7}.
(1)
Both are open sets, and their intersection is U∩V=X∖{1,2,3,5,7,8}. Thus 4,6,9,10,… are in both. Their finite exclusions cannot separate the infinite remainder. The finite intersection of any finite collection of nonempty open sets is again a nonempty open set, since its complement is a finite union of finite sets. An arbitrary nonempty union is open because its complement is contained in the finite complement of any one nonempty member.
The cofinite topology is useful for separating hypotheses that familiar metric spaces package together. An infinite cofinite topological space is a T1 space, because its singletons are closed, but is not a Hausdorff space, because two nonempty open sets cannot be disjoint sets. It is a hyperconnected space and hence a connected space. Moreover, every subset of a cofinite space is compact, and sequence convergence in the cofinite topology can have many limits. These are compatible properties, rather than contradictions: the usual uniqueness and closedness results use the Hausdorff space hypothesis.[ref]

By convergence of a sequence in a topological space, xn​→a means that every open neighbourhood of a contains all sufficiently late terms. In the cofinite topology, this is equivalent to the condition that, for every b=a, the value b occurs only finitely often. Necessity uses the open neighbourhood X∖{b}; sufficiency chooses an index beyond every last occurrence of the finitely many points excluded by a given open neighbourhood.
Consequently a sequence with distinct terms converges to every point of X. For the original choice xn​=n on X=N>0​, take the two open neighbourhoods
U1​=X∖{2,5,8}∋1,U2​=X∖{1,3,7}∋2.
(2)
All terms with n≥9 lie in U1​ and all terms with n≥8 lie in U2​. More generally, each finite excluded set has a last visit, so xn​→1 and xn​→2, and in fact xn​→a for every a∈X. No numerical distance is tending to zero here; the open sets specify the meaning of convergence.
Distinct terms are sufficient, not necessary. The sequence 1,1,2,2,3,3,… also converges to every point, since each value occurs only twice. By contrast, the constant sequence xn​=1 converges only to 1: an open neighbourhood of any a=1 can exclude 1. The alternating sequence 1,2,1,2,… converges to no point, since some value different from any proposed limit occurs infinitely often.

To see the finite reduction directly, take an open cover of a nonempty A by open sets of X and choose one member U containing a point of A. Since U has finite complement, the set A∖U is finite. Choose a covering member for each of those remaining points. Those members together with U are a finite subcover. The empty set is already compact.
Equivalently, the subspace topology on A is itself cofinite: for finite F⊆X, the trace of X∖F is A∖(F∩A). The argument applies again inside A. A concrete open cover {X∖{k}:k∈X} of X=N>0​ needs only the two members X∖{1} and X∖{2} when these labels are distinct: each fills the other's single gap.
On X=N>0​, the subset of even integers is compact but not closed, because it is infinite and proper. A compact subset of a Hausdorff space is guaranteed to be closed, whereas compactness without the Hausdorff space assumption does not suffice. Changing the topology changes compactness: the same infinite set with its discrete topology has the singleton open cover, which has no finite subcover. The finite-exception argument is special to finite complements; in the cocountable topology, compact subsets of a cocountable space must instead be finite.

For example, f(n)=n from N>0​ with its cofinite topology into the real line with its usual Euclidean metric is not continuous: the inverse image of the open interval (1/2,3/2) is {1}, which is not open in the infinite domain. Topology OurBigBook.com
A subset F of a topological space (X,τ) is closed when its complement in that same ambient space is open: X∖F∈τ. For example, the closed interval [0,1] is closed in the usual real line because its complement is the open set (−∞,0)∪(1,∞). Always specify the ambient topological space: a subset can be closed in a subspace topology without being closed in the surrounding space. [ref]
Being closed is not the logical negation of being open. In the usual real line, all four combinations occur: (0,1) is open but not closed; [0,1] is closed but not open; the half-open interval [0,1) is neither open nor closed; and both the empty set and the whole real line are open and closed, hence clopen. Nor does being closed imply being a bounded set: [0,∞) is closed because its complement (−∞,0) is open, but it is not a bounded set. The symbol ∞ is not an extra point that this interval must contain.
The coloured strokes mark membership; filled endpoint circles mean included points, and hollow endpoint circles mean excluded points. The empty set has no coloured points, while arrows at both ends of the coloured real line indicate that membership continues indefinitely. These examples use the usual topology of the real line.
In a metric space X, a subset F is closed exactly when every convergent sequence (xn​) in F whose limit of a sequence x lies in X has x∈F. For example, xn​=1−1/n lies in [0,1) for n≥1 and has limit of a sequence 1, which is missing; thus this half-open interval is not closed in the real line. This criterion is useful for keeping limiting constructions inside a prescribed set. [ref]
In every topological space, the general criterion is F=F, using closure; equivalently, F contains all its limit points. A closed set is always a sequentially closed set, but the converse can fail outside metric spaces. Arbitrary intersections and finite unions of closed sets are closed, by taking complements in the topology axioms.

The closure turns an arbitrary subset into a closed set with no unnecessary added points. It satisfies A⊆A and A=A; a subset is closed exactly when A=A. Quotient topology

Words: 777 Articles: 5
Topology OurBigBook.com
The quotient topology turns an instruction to glue points together into a precise topological space. Start with a topological space (X,τX​) and an equivalence relation ∼. The quotient set X/∼ consists of equivalence classes, and its canonical projection of a quotient set is
q:X⟶X/∼,q(x)=[x].
(10)
The quotient topology is defined by the rule using preimages of open sets:
τq​={U⊆X/∼:q−1(U)∈τX​}.
(11)
Thus a subset of the quotient space is open if and only if its entire preimage is open in X. Each fiber q−1({[x]}) is the whole equivalence class [x], so the preimage includes every point glued to any of its members.[ref]
This is the finest topology making q a continuous map: every topology with that property can contain only subsets whose preimages are open. It really is a topology, because preimages preserve the empty set, the whole set, arbitrary unions, and finite intersections. The gluing example below shows why checking a complete preimage matters, especially at the seam.
The quotient topology also makes continuous maps out of a glued space easy to construct. A continuous map f:X→Z descends to a unique continuous map fˉ​:X/∼→Z exactly when it is constant on every fiber of q, meaning x∼y⇒f(x)=f(y). Define fˉ​([x])=f(x); the equivalence class representative cannot affect the answer. For every open set V⊆Z,
q−1(fˉ​−1(V))=f−1(V).
(12)
The right side is open, so the quotient topology makes fˉ​−1(V) open. Conversely, if f=fˉ​∘q for a continuous map fˉ​, then composition of continuous functions makes f continuous, and equal equivalence classes force equal values. This is the universal property of the quotient topology. [ref]
A surjective continuous map is not automatically a quotient map. On the same two-point set D={a,b}, take the identity map from the discrete topology to the indiscrete topology. It is continuous and surjective, but {a} is not open in the target even though its preimage is open in the domain. The quotient topology for this identity map would be the discrete topology. Thus continuity supplies only one direction of the rule using preimages of open sets; a quotient map requires both.

Quotient topological space (X/∼)

Words: 341
Quotient topology OurBigBook.com
A quotient topological space is a quotient set equipped with the quotient topology. For a concrete gluing, give the closed interval I=[0,1] its usual subspace topology, identify 0∼1, and leave every interior point in its own singleton equivalence class. The resulting quotient space is a circle: the two endpoints become one point, while interior points remain distinct.
The exact continuous map to the unit circle in the plane is
p(t)=(cos(2πt),sin(2πt)),pˉ​([t])=p(t).
(13)
Here sine and cosine give p(0)=p(1)=(1,0), and p(s)=p(t) holds exactly when s=t or {s,t}={0,1}. Thus p induces a bijection pˉ​:I/∼→S1. [ref] The universal property of the quotient topology makes pˉ​ continuous. The quotient of a compact space is compact, and the unit circle is Hausdorff, so the compact-to-Hausdorff continuous bijection theorem makes pˉ​ a homeomorphism. This verifies the topology, not merely the point identifications.
To inspect an open neighbourhood of the seam, choose 0<ε<1/2 and let Uε​=p([0,ε)∪(1−ε,1]). Its full preimage is
p−1(Uε​)=[0,ε)∪(1−ε,1].
(14)
Both pieces are open in the subspace topology on I, so Uε​ is open in the circle. In contrast, A=[0,ε) is open in I, but
p−1(p(A))=[0,ε)∪{1}
(15)
is not open in I: it contains 1 without any neighbourhood of 1. Hence p(A) is not open in the circle. A quotient map can therefore fail to be an open map.
For a continuous function f:I→R, the only gluing condition is f(0)=f(1). For example, f(t)=cos(2πt) defines a continuous function on the circle, whereas f(t)=t does not. This lets us use an interval as a coordinate for a periodic function while making the seam invisible. More general quotient spaces encode glued geometric pieces in the same way: describe continuous maps before gluing and check that their values agree on every equivalence class.
The Hausdorff property need not survive a quotient topology. In the non-Hausdorff quotient of the real line by rational translation, x∼y means x−y∈Q. A nonempty open preimage W must contain all translates by rational numbers of any open interval inside it. The density of the rational numbers then forces W=R: for any y, some rational number r has y−r in that interval. Thus this quotient space has the indiscrete topology. The irrationality of the square root of two gives distinct equivalence classes for 0 and 2​, so this quotient space is not Hausdorff. Unlike the endpoint-gluing circle, this gluing identifies a dense subset with each point.

Compact space

Words: 2k Articles: 15
Topology OurBigBook.com
A topological space X is compact when every open cover has a finite subcover: whenever open sets Ui​ satisfy X=⋃i∈I​Ui​, some finite selection satisfies X=Ui1​​∪⋯∪Uim​​. A subset K of an ambient topological space is compact when its subspace topology is compact; equivalently, every open cover of K by ambient open sets has a finite subcover. The word every matters: finding one finite subcover of one open cover is not enough to establish compactness. [ref]
The closed interval [0,1] is compact by the Heine-Borel theorem. For a concrete open cover, take the three open intervals (−0.1,0.45), (0.35,0.8), and (0.7,1.1). Their union is (−0.1,1.1), so they cover every point of [0,1], including both endpoints. The overlaps have lengths 0.1 and 0.1, leaving no gaps. Each member is necessary for this particular open cover: removing them respectively leaves 0, 0.5, or 1 uncovered.
Above, hollow markers denote the excluded endpoints of the covering open intervals, while the solid endpoints belong to the covered closed interval. Below, each displayed open interval is one member of an infinite open cover of (0,1); finitely many rows always leave points near zero uncovered. The rows are vertically separated for readability and all refer to the same real line.
The open interval (0,1) is a bounded set but is not compact: the open sets
Un​=(1/n,1),n≥2,
(20)
give an open cover of (0,1), since every 0<x<1 has 1/n<x for sufficiently large n. These are also open sets for the subspace topology on (0,1). Any nonempty finite selection has a largest index N, so its union is just (1/N,1) and misses the point 1/(N+1), which still belongs to (0,1). Thus no finite subcover exists, however many members we select. The same family is not an open cover of [0,1], since it misses both endpoints.
In a metric space, compactness is equivalent to sequential compactness: every sequence in the subset has a convergent subsequence whose limit of a sequence belongs to that subset. This equivalence does not extend to all topological spaces. For example, xn​=1/n for n≥2 has limit of a sequence zero in [0,1]. The same sequence lies in (0,1), but every subsequence still has limit of a sequence zero on the real line, so no subsequence converges to a point of (0,1). Merely approaching a boundary is harmless when the required point remains available. [ref]
Both panels show the sequence xn​=1/n for n≥2 approaching zero. In the closed interval, zero is an allowed limit of a sequence; in the open interval, the hollow marker identifies the missing point. This single sequence disproves sequential compactness of (0,1); compactness of [0,1] still requires control of every open cover or every sequence, supplied by the Heine-Borel theorem.
An infinite set with the discrete topology similarly fails compactness, using the open cover by all its singletons. Every finite set is compact in any topology: select one covering open set for each point. The empty set is compact because the empty selection is a finite subcover. This open cover definition does not require the topological space to be Hausdorff; in algebraic geometry it is often called quasi-compactness.
The beauty of compactness is that information valid around each point can often be controlled using finitely many regions. A finite subcover lets us combine finitely many local bounds, or choose the smallest of finitely many positive tolerances, to obtain control across the whole compact space. This is why compactness repeatedly turns approximation into existence and why it is so useful in optimization through the extreme value theorem.
Every closed set in a compact space is compact, and a continuous image of a compact space is compact. The latter proof pulls an open cover back by inverse images, selects a finite subcover, and maps forward. This makes compactness useful for proving existence: the extreme value theorem guarantees that a continuous function from a nonempty compact space to the real line attains both a minimum and a maximum. For example, q(x)=x(1−x)=1/4−(x−1/2)2 on [0,1] has maximum 1/4 at 1/2 and minimum zero at its endpoints. On (0,1) its infimum is still zero but is never attained. [ref]

Ultrafilter characterization of compactness

Words: 95
Compact space OurBigBook.com
A topological space is compact if and only if every ultrafilter on it converges to at least one point, assuming the ultrafilter lemma. No Hausdorff assumption is needed. In a compact space, the closures of the filter members have the finite intersection property, so choose a point in their intersection. Every open neighbourhood of that point belongs to the ultrafilter, since otherwise its closed complement would be a filter member. Conversely, extend the complements of a cover with no finite subcover to an ultrafilter; a limit point lies in a covering open set, contradicting the simultaneous membership of that set and its complement.

Let continuous maps f,g:X⇉Y between compact Hausdorff spaces have an underlying split coequalizer q:Y→Z with set maps s,t satisfying qs=1, ft=1 and gt=sq. Its equivalence relation is the image of the closed subset {(x,x′)∈X2:g(x)=g(x′)} under (f,f). One inclusion follows from qf=qg; for the other use x=t(y) and x′=t(y′) whenever q(y)=q(y′). This image is compact and hence closed in the Hausdorff product Y2. The quotient is therefore compact Hausdorff, giving the preserved coequalizer required by the Beck monadicity theorem.

Compact Hausdorff space OurBigBook.com
Embed N into the compact product {0,1}P(N) by j(n)S​=1S​(n) and take its closure X. The Tychonoff theorem makes X a compact Hausdorff space, while j(N) is countable, dense and discrete in its subspace topology. Yet X is not metrizable. Any convergent subsequence j(nk​) of distinct points would have a convergent coordinate for S={n2​,n4​,…}, whereas that coordinate alternates between zero and one. This contradicts sequential compactness of a compact metric space. Thus a dense metrizable subspace does not force a separable compact Hausdorff ambient space to be metrizable.

Heine-Borel theorem (K⊆Rd:K compact⟺K closed and bounded)

Words: 322
Compact space OurBigBook.com
For every finite d≥1, a subset K⊆Rd of Euclidean space is compact if and only if it is a closed set and a bounded set. Here closed means closed in the ambient Euclidean space, not merely in K itself, and the bounded set condition uses the Euclidean norm. The empty set is included: it is a closed set, a bounded set, and compact. [ref]
This makes an apparently infinite test practical. To verify compactness of a closed interval [a,b] with finite endpoints, we need not examine every open cover: it is closed in the real line and a bounded set. By contrast, the open interval (0,1) is a bounded set but is not closed in the real line, as the missing-endpoint figure in compact space illustrates. The whole real line is closed but is not a bounded set, so it too fails compactness. These examples show why both hypotheses are needed.
The same criterion holds in any real or complex finite-dimensional vector space equipped with a norm: all norms there are equivalent norms, so they give the same open sets, closed sets, and bounded sets. Since compactness depends only on the topology, choosing a different norm does not change the conclusion. Without an appropriate topology, a bare vector space alone has no notion of compactness.
The restriction to a finite-dimensional vector space is essential. In the l2 sequence space, an infinite-dimensional vector space that is also a Hilbert space, let en​ be the vectors of its standard orthonormal basis. All lie in the closed unit ball B={x:∥x∥≤1}, which is a closed set and a bounded set in the norm topology. For distinct indices, their inner product is zero, giving
∥en​−em​∥2=∥en​∥2+∥em​∥2−2Re⟨en​,em​⟩=2.
(21)
Thus distinct terms remain distance 2​ apart. No subsequence is a Cauchy sequence, hence none is a convergent sequence. The equivalence of compactness and sequential compactness in a metric space proves that this closed unit ball is not compact. The conclusion concerns the norm topology.
A short proof outline in Euclidean space explains the role of a finite-dimensional vector space. For a sequence in a bounded set, apply the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem to each of the Cartesian coordinates in turn, retaining a subsequence at each of the finitely many steps. The final subsequence is a convergent sequence in all Cartesian coordinates, and a closed set contains its limit of a sequence. This yields sequential compactness, hence compactness. Conversely, a compact subset of a metric space is a closed set and a bounded set. [ref]

Continuous image of a compact space

Words: 316
Compact space OurBigBook.com
Let X,Y be topological spaces, let X be compact, and let f:X→Y be a continuous map. Then its image f(X) is compact with the subspace topology inherited from Y. More generally, a continuous map sends every compact subset K⊆X to a compact subset f(K)⊆Y, by applying the same statement to its restriction to K. Neither X nor Y needs to be Hausdorff.[ref]
For example, the polynomial function f(x)=x2 sends the compact closed interval [0,1] onto [0,1]. The open intervals V1​=(−1/10,16/25) and V2​=(9/25,11/10) give an open cover of the image. Their inverse images in the domain are
f−1(V1​)=[0,4/5),f−1(V2​)=(3/5,1].
(22)
Both are open sets in the subspace topology of [0,1], even though neither is an open set in the ambient real line. They cover the domain, so the corresponding two target open sets cover the image.
Matching colors identify the target open sets and their inverse images. Filled endpoints are included and hollow endpoints excluded. This particular open cover illustrates the mechanism; compactness requires a finite subcover for every open cover.
For the general proof, write an arbitrary open cover of f(X) as {f(X)∩Vi​:i∈I} with each Vi​ an open set in Y. By continuity, the inverse images f−1(Vi​) form an open cover of X. Its compactness provides indices i1​,…,im​ such that
X=⋃j=1m​f−1(Vij​​)⟹f(X)⊆⋃j=1m​Vij​​.
(23)
This gives the required finite subcover of f(X). The argument uses inverse images because continuous maps need not send open sets to open sets. For the empty set, the empty selection suffices.
The image of a compact Hausdorff space under a continuous map need not itself be Hausdorff. Take D={0,1} with the discrete topology and S={0,1} with the Sierpiński space topology {∅,{1},S}. The identity map D→S is a continuous bijection, since the inverse image of every target open set is an open set in D. Its image is compact, but the two points of S have no disjoint open neighborhoods. If the target Y is Hausdorff, its subspace topology does make f(X) Hausdorff, and the compact subset of a Hausdorff space theorem also makes f(X) closed in Y.
The practical payoff is existence: the extreme value theorem uses the compact image of a nonempty compact space under a real-valued continuous function to obtain an attained minimum and maximum. When f is also a bijection onto a Hausdorff target, the compact-to-Hausdorff continuous bijection theorem supplies continuity of its inverse without a separate formula.

Compact subset of a Hausdorff space

Hausdorff space OurBigBook.com
Let K⊆X, where the ambient topological space X is Hausdorff and K is compact in its subspace topology. Then K is a closed set in X: the complement X∖K is an open set in X. The ambient space need not be compact. For example, [0,1] is a compact closed interval in the non-compact Hausdorff real line.[ref]
The ambient Hausdorff hypothesis matters even when K itself is Hausdorff. In the Sierpiński space S={0,1}, the open sets are ∅,{1},S, so the closed sets are ∅,{0},S. Thus K={1} is compact and Hausdorff in its one-point subspace topology, but is not closed in S: its complement {0} is not an open set. Every open neighborhood of 0 contains 1, so separation from K fails. In contrast, the discrete topology on the same underlying set is Hausdorff and makes both singletons closed.
The diagram lists every open set and closed set, so the distinction can be checked directly. All subsets in both panels are compact: for any open cover of a finite set, choose one covering open set per point, obtaining a finite subcover. Compactness alone therefore cannot distinguish the two panels.
Here is the finite-selection mechanism in the general proof. For x∈X∖K and each k∈K, the Hausdorff property gives disjoint open neighborhoods Uk​ of k and Vk​ of x. The Uk​ give an ambient open cover of K. Select a finite subcover Uk1​​,…,Ukm​​ and set
U=⋃j=1m​Ukj​​,V=⋂j=1m​Vkj​​.
(24)
Then K⊆U, x∈V, and U∩V=∅. The finite intersection makes V an open set; an infinite intersection would not guarantee this. Thus every point of X∖K has an open neighborhood contained in that complement, proving that K is closed. The empty set is already closed.
This theorem combines with the continuous image of a compact space theorem to make every continuous map from a compact space to a Hausdorff space a closed map: a closed subset of its domain is compact, and its image is compact and hence closed in the target. This is the reason the inverse in the compact-to-Hausdorff continuous bijection theorem is continuous. The converse implication, from closed to compact, needs additional hypotheses: the real line is closed in itself but not compact; in a compact space, every closed subset is compact.

Topology OurBigBook.com
A homeomorphism is a bijection between topological spaces such that both f and f−1 are continuous maps. Equivalently, for every subset U⊆X, U is an open set if and only if f(U) is an open set in Y. A homeomorphism therefore transports the entire topology, including connectedness and compactness. It need not preserve numerical metric values, and a bounded set need not map to a bounded set.
For example, an explicit homeomorphism between an open interval and the real line is
f:(0,1)→R,f(x)=tan(π(x−1/2)),f−1(y)=21​+πarctany​.
(25)
The tangent function on (−π/2,π/2) is strictly increasing and takes every real value; the displayed arctangent inverse verifies the bijection. Both formulas define continuous maps on their stated domains. Computed values are f(1/4)=−1, f(1/2)=0, and f(3/4)=1. Points approach infinity as x approaches an excluded endpoint. Thus a bounded set can have the same topology as an unbounded one; neither of these topological spaces is compact.
A useful shortcut is the compact-to-Hausdorff continuous bijection theorem: a continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism. Its images of closed sets are compact sets, hence closed sets in the target, which proves continuity of the inverse. The indiscrete topology example shows why the Hausdorff assumption matters. [ref]

This illustrates how a simple connectedness test can rule out every possible homeomorphism.

Logarithmic spiral OurBigBook.com
The map h is a homeomorphism from the real line to its image with the subspace topology: its continuous inverse is h−1(x,y)=logx2+y2​. Different parameters have different radii, so winding does not destroy injectivity. The origin is an accumulation point of the spiral but is not a point of this space.

Simple curve

Words: 20
Curve OurBigBook.com
A simple curve is an injective curve, apart from the permitted coincidence of its two endpoints when it is closed.

Space-filling curve

Words: 19
Curve OurBigBook.com
A space-filling curve is a surjective continuous map from an interval onto a region of dimension at least two.

Topology OurBigBook.com

Knaster-Kuratowski-Mazurkiewicz lemma

Words: 110 Articles: 3
Topology OurBigBook.com
For a simplex with vertices indexed by 0,…,n, let closed sets Fi​ have the property that every face spanned by an index set I lies in ⋃i∈I​Fi​. Then ⋂i=0n​Fi​ is nonempty. The triangle KKM lemma is a two-dimensional covering formulation of this simplex-intersection principle.

Triangle KKM lemma

Words: 66 Articles: 2
Knaster-Kuratowski-Mazurkiewicz lemma OurBigBook.com
If three closed sets cover a triangle and respectively contain its three opposite sides, then their triple intersection is nonempty.

Distance-function barycentric map

Words: 26
Triangle KKM lemma OurBigBook.com
Normalized distances to three closed sets give continuous barycentric coordinates; a covering forces at least one coordinate to vanish, placing the image on the simplex boundary.

No-retraction covering principle

Words: 20
Triangle KKM lemma OurBigBook.com
A closed-cover intersection statement for a simplex is equivalent to the nonexistence of a boundary-valued map that preserves every face.
